Models S7 to S10 (@tbl-models-s7s10) were next fitted with the observed data. Diagnostic statistics indicated that the HMC algorithm converges with satisfactory results (@tbl-diagnostic-summary-s8s10). @fig-chain-stats-s7s10-org shows per-parameter summaries of $\hat{R}$ and effective sample size indicating that parameters have $\hat{R} < 1.01$ and that bulk effective sample sizes are generally > 1000 per chain (minimum about 680 per chain, in model s9).

|Model |Likelihood |Variance structure  |
|---|---|---|
|`s7`|Univariate normal    |Time- and type-specific &sigma;|
|`s8`|Multivariate normal  |Time- and type-specific &sigma;|
|`s9`|Univariate normal    |Time-, type-, and treat-specific &sigma;|
|`s10`|Multivariate normal |Time-, type-, and treat-specific &sigma;|

: Summary of model configurations {#tbl-models-s7s10}

```{r}
               values_to = "value",

    pivot_longer(cols = HDL:LDL,

  mutate(value_std = if_else(analyte %in% c("TG", "HOMA2IR", "HbA1c"), log(value), value)) |>

         value_std = (value_std - mean(value_std, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(value_std, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 

  mutate(participant = paste0("p", participant))
```

```{r}
# Extract relevant variables for summary statistics
extract_sum <- function(fit) {
  
  all_vars <- fit$metadata()$variables
  keep <- setdiff(
    all_vars,
    grep("^(lp__|y|y_rep|y_expect|y_impute|pre|pre_impute|pre_wide|
                 y_wide_1|y_wide_2|mu_wide_1|mu_wide_2|mu|sig|
                 log_lik_part|diagnosed|n_criteria)\\[",
         all_vars, value = TRUE)
  )
  sum <- fit$summary(variables = keep, .cores = 12)
  return(sum)
  
}

fits <- list(fit.s7.post,

             fit.s9.post,
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diagnostic-summary-s8s10
#| tbl-cap: "Diagnostic summaries of models s7 to s10. BFMI, Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information."


diag_sum <- function(fit) {
  
  ds <- fit$diagnostic_summary()
  
  ds_df <- data.frame(
    chain = 1:length(ds$num_divergent),
    divergent = ds$num_divergent, 
    max_treedepth = ds$num_max_treedepth, 
    ebfmi = round(ds$ebfmi, 2) 
             )
  
  return(ds_df)
  
}

diagsums <- lapply(fits, diag_sum)
models <- rep(paste0("s", 7:10), each = 4)
  
bind_rows(diagsums) |> 
  mutate(model = models) |> 
  select(model, chain:ebfmi) |> 
  group_by(model) |> 
  gt() |> 
  cols_label(
    model = "Model", 
    chain = "Chain",
    divergent = "n divergent trans.", 
    max_treedepth = "n maximum treedepth", 
    ebfmi = "BFMI")
  




```

Using the observed data set we are next assessing the models tendencies to produce replicated data similar to the observed data. All models (s7-s10) are still considered in these posterior predictive checks. The overall distributions of replicated data (y^rep^) tend to look very similar to the observed data for each measurement type, treatment, and time-point combinations in all considered models (@fig-ppcheck-dist-s7, @fig-ppcheck-dist-s8, @fig-ppcheck-dist-s9, @fig-ppcheck-dist-s10).


```{r}

yrep.s9 <- fit.s9.post$draws("y_rep", format = "df")

# Distribution of observed values vs. distribution of y rep
ppcheck_dist <- function(yreps, obsdata, label = FALSE) {
  
  # For the caption 
  caption <- str_wrap(paste("Type labels: ", 
                   paste0(labels$type, ",", labels$label, collapse = "; ")))
  
  
  
  # Set number of draws for posterior predictive checks
  # and sample from random draw
  ndraws <- 40
  randraw <- sample(1:(max(yreps$.draw)), ndraws)
  
  p <- yreps |> 
  filter(.draw %in% randraw) |> 
  pivot_longer(starts_with("y_rep")) |> 
  mutate(
    miss_pre = rep(d$pre_miss, ndraws),
    miss = rep(d$y_miss, ndraws),
    type = rep(d$type, ndraws), 
    sex = rep(ifelse(d$sex == -0.5, "m", "f"), ndraws),
    treat = rep(d$treat, ndraws), 
    time = rep(d$time, ndraws),
  ) |> 
    # Filter simulations not corresponding to observed data
    # Filter away missing data obs
    filter(miss == 1, 
           miss_pre == 1) |> 
    
  ggplot(aes(value)) + 
  geom_line(stat = "density", 
            aes(color = sex, group = paste(.draw, sex)),
            alpha = 0.2) + 
  facet_grid(time + treat ~ type, 
             labeller = label_both, 
             scales = "free") +
  
  geom_line(data = obsdata, 
            aes(y, group = NULL, color = sex), 
            stat = "density", 
     
            alpha = 0.8,
            linewidth = 1.2) +
  alpha_theme(yaxis = FALSE) + 
    scale_color_manual(values = colscale[c(1, 3)]) +
  theme(axis.title.y =  element_blank()) + 
    labs(x = "y^rep^ and observed values", 
         color = "Sex")  +
    theme(axis.title.x = element_markdown(), 
          axis.title.y = element_blank()) 
  
  if(label) {
    p <- p + labs(caption = caption)
            }

  return(p)

}


# Posterior predictive check. the function can be used for a summary statistics
# function (sd, mean, max, min, quantile).
# use stat_arg for supplying extra functions to the summary function.
ppcheck_stat <- function(yreps, obsdata,
                         stat = sd,
                         stat_arg = list(),
                         group = c("type", "time", "treat"),
                         fill_color = "treat",
                         plot = TRUE) {

  if (obsdata$sex[1] %in% c(-0.5, 0.5)) stop("Convert sex to a factor with 'm' and 'f'")
  if (!fill_color %in% group) stop("`fill_color` must be one of `group`")

  sumstat <- obsdata |>
    summarise(.by = all_of(group),
              s = do.call(stat, c(list(y), stat_arg)))

  ndraws <- nrow(yreps)
  caption <- paste("Type labels: ",
                   paste0(labels$type, ", ", labels$label, collapse = ";\n"))

  y_rep_data <- yreps |>
    filter(.draw %in% 1:ndraws) |>
    pivot_longer(starts_with("y_rep")) |>
    mutate(
      miss     = rep(d$y_miss,   ndraws),
      miss_pre = rep(d$pre_miss, ndraws),
      type     = rep(d$type,     ndraws),
      sex      = rep(ifelse(d$sex == -0.5, "m", "f"), ndraws),
      treat    = rep(d$treat,    ndraws),
      time     = rep(d$time,     ndraws),
      sex      = factor(sex, levels = c("m", "f"))
    ) |>
    filter(miss == 1, miss_pre == 1) |>
    summarise(.by = all_of(c(".draw", group)),
              s = do.call(stat, c(list(value), stat_arg)))

  pvals <- y_rep_data |>
    rename(srep = s) |>
    inner_join(sumstat) |>
    summarise(.by = all_of(group), pval = mean(srep >= s)) |>
    mutate(direction = if_else(pval > 0.5, "over", "under"),
           pval = pmin(pval, 1 - pval)) |>
    arrange(pval)

  if(plot) {
     plot1 <- y_rep_data |>
    ggplot(aes(s, color = as.factor(.data[[fill_color]]))) +

       geom_line(stat = "density") +
    facet_grid(type ~ time, labeller = label_both, scales = "free") +
    alpha_theme(yaxis = FALSE) +
    geom_vline(data = sumstat,
               aes(xintercept = s, color = as.factor(.data[[fill_color]]))) +
    scale_color_manual(values = colscale) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colscale) +
    labs(x = "Test statistic",
         color = as.factor(fill_color), fill = as.factor(fill_color),
         subtitle = "Estimates (T(y^rep^) and T(y^obs^))",
         caption = caption) +
    theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
          plot.subtitle = element_markdown())

  plot2 <- y_rep_data |>
    rename(srep = s) |>
    inner_join(sumstat) |>
    mutate(t_diff = srep - s) |>
    ggplot(aes(t_diff, color = as.factor(.data[[fill_color]]))) +
    geom_line(stat = "density") +
    facet_grid(type ~ time, labeller = label_both, scales = "free") +
    alpha_theme(yaxis = FALSE) +
    scale_color_manual(values = colscale) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colscale) +
    labs(x = "Contrast", fill = fill_color,
         subtitle = "Contrast (T(y^rep^) - T(y^obs^))",
         caption = caption) +
    theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(),
          plot.subtitle = element_markdown()) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2, color = "gray")

  return(list(plot_estimate = plot1, plot_contrast = plot2, pvals = pvals))

  } else {
    return(pvals)
  }



}

p1 <- ppcheck_dist(yrep.s7, dobs) + labs(subtitle = "Model s7")

p2 <- ppcheck_dist(yrep.s8, dobs)+ labs(subtitle = "Model s8")

p3 <- ppcheck_dist(yrep.s9, dobs)+ labs(subtitle = "Model s9")

p4 <- ppcheck_dist(yrep.s10, dobs, label = TRUE)+ labs(subtitle = "Model s10")
```

Combining all comparisons between replicated and observed data as p-values indicate that models s8 and s10 tend to have more examples of "extreme" observed data compared to model implications (p-values closer to 0 in @fig-pval-s7-s10-ppcheck). No systematic under- or over-estimation is evident in any model.

Next we compute the approximate leave-one-out cross-validation statistics from the models using Pareto smoothed importance sampling [@vehtari2017]. As a first step we only consider the Pareto k diagnostic values as these indirectly indicates observations that are influential for the models. Here, one observation corresponds to a participant, i.e., all values corresponding to a participant contribute to the log-likelihood. The multivariate models have more unstable estimates of the Pareto k statistic, indicating that these models are "more surprised" by single observations (@fig-paretok-s7s10). 

Together with the indications from above that suggest that the multivariate models (and more so the heteroscedastic variant, s10) tend to under or overestimate group-specific variation in replicate simulations we will consider a more robust definition of the two model classes (uni- and multivariate models).
<!-- REVIEW: This contradicts the preceding paragraph, which states "No systematic under or over-estimation are evident in either model"; what the p-values show is more "extreme" observed SDs in s8 and s10, not a directional bias. Suggested: "Together with the indications from above that the multivariate models (and more so the heteroscedastic variant, s10) more often produce observed SDs that are extreme relative to the replicated data, we will consider a more robust definition of the two model classes (uni- and multivariate models)." -->

Although high Pareto k values indicate unreliable estimates of the expected log-pointwise predictive density we finally compare models for their out-of-sample predictive performance (@tbl-loo-s7s10). These estimates indicate that multivariate models would predict better on new data with no differences between models with different residual variance structures.



```{r}
#| eval: true
#| label: fig-paretok-s7s10
#| fig-cap: "Pareto k statistic for participants with complete data in each model."
# Check log likelihood 



loo.s7 <- readRDS("fits/paper1/loo_s7.RDS")
loo.s8 <- readRDS("fits/paper1/loo_s8.RDS")
loo.s9 <- readRDS("fits/paper1/loo_s9.RDS")
loo.s10 <-readRDS("fits/paper1/loo_s10.RDS")





bind_rows(
  loo.s7$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s7"), 
    loo.s8$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s8"), 
    loo.s9$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s9"), 
    loo.s10$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s10")) |> 
  
  mutate(id = gsub("log_lik_part\\[", "", id), 
         id = gsub("\\]", "", id), 
         flag = if_else(influence_pareto_k > 0.7, "flag", "noflag"), 
         model = factor(model, levels = c("s7", "s9", "s8", "s10"))) |> 
  
  ggplot(aes(id, influence_pareto_k, color = model, shape = model,  alpha = flag)) + 
  geom_point(size = 3) + 
  alpha_theme() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(colscale[1], colscale[1], colscale[2], colscale[2])) + 
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16,17,16,17)) + 
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(1, 0.3), guide = "none") + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.7, lty = 2) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), 
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) + 
  labs(color = "Model",
       shape = "Model",
       x = "Participant (complete cases)", 
       y = "Pareto k influence")

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-loo-s7s10
#| tbl-cap: "ELPD estimate differences from models s7-s10."


loo_compare(list("s7" = loo.s7, 
                 "s8" = loo.s8, 
                 "s9" = loo.s9, 
                 "s10" = loo.s10))  |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "Model") |> 
  dplyr::select(Model, elpd_diff, se_diff) |> 
  gt() |> 
  cols_label(elpd_diff = 'ELPD diff', 
             se_diff = "SE") |> 
  fmt_auto()

```




### Model expansion: Robust likelihood

As our initial models might suggest that they are "surprised" by specific data point we will consider a heavy-tailed likelihood to allow for inference robust to extreme observations. The Student's t-distribution is available both as a uni- and multivariate definition. Models s11 and s12 are updated from s9 and s10 to the Student-t versions of these model specifications. In model s11, the relevant change is in the definition of the likelihood ($y_i \sim \operatorname{Student-t}(\mu_i, \sigma_i, \nu)$. The $\nu$ parameter is set to 4 (as pragmatic starting point, separating it from the normal likelihood [@gelman2014 p. 442]). In model s12 the likelihood is updated to a multivariate Student's t-distribution $y_i \sim \operatorname{MVT}(\mu_i, \Sigma, \nu)$, also with $\nu$ set to 4.

To isolate the contribution of the correlation structure under the t-distributed likelihood, model s18 is the univariate counterpart of s13: a univariate Student-t likelihood with $\nu = 4$ and the same time &times; type structure of $\sigma$, but no correlation among measurement types. s18 thus relates to s13 as s7 relates to s8, and to s11 as s7 relates to s9.

### Simplification of the correlation structure 

A new set of models simplifies the correlation structure. Instead of estimating the full $M \times M$ correlation matrix with an LKJ prior (as in models s8-s13, where $M = 2K$ is the number of measurement types stacked over the two post-intervention time points), this set of models relates each outcome to a small number of latent variables, following the factor approach used in the simulations (@sec-synth-data; see also [the Stan User Guide](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/missing-data.html#loading-matrix-for-factor-analysis)). Each measurement type at each time point is given a loading onto $D$ latent factors, collected in a $M \times D$ loading matrix $\Lambda$, together with a vector $\psi$ of length $M$ containing idiosyncratic (factor-unexplained) standard deviations on the standardised correlation scale, $\psi \sim \operatorname{LogNormal}(\log(0.6), 0.4)$. The time &times; treat &times; type (s14, s15) or time &times; type (s16, s17) structure of the residual variation is instead carried by the residual scales $\sigma$. Rows $1$ to $K$ of $\Lambda$ hold the loadings for the first post-intervention time point and rows $K+1$ to $M$ the loadings for the second. Because the two blocks of rows are estimated separately, the within-time correlation structures are free to differ between time points, whereas the between-time correlations are restricted to correlations induced by factor loadings. The implied correlation matrix is obtained by normalising the factor covariance to unit diagonal, and the covariance matrix is then built from the Cholesky factor of this correlation matrix and the residual scales $\sigma$:

$$
\begin{align}
\Sigma_\text{raw} &= \Lambda \Lambda^T + \operatorname{diag}(\psi^2) \\
R &= \operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_\text{raw})^{-1/2} \, \Sigma_\text{raw} \, \operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_\text{raw})^{-1/2} \\
L_R &= \operatorname{chol}(R) \\
L_\Sigma &= \operatorname{diag}(\sigma) L_R \\
\Sigma &= L_\Sigma L_\Sigma^T
\end{align}
$$

Since $R$ has unit diagonal, $\sigma$ keeps its interpretation as the marginal residual standard deviation for each time $\times$ type (s16 and s17) or time $\times$ type $\times$ treatment (s14 and s15) combination, exactly as in the models with a full correlation matrix. Only the correlation part is constrained to a low-rank structure (low-rank in the meaning that the correlation matrix is informed by a smaller number of loadings). The factor model is not identified with respect to rotations of $\Lambda$, as any orthogonal rotation of the factors leaves $\Lambda \Lambda^T$ unchanged. Following @geweke1996 [p. 565], we therefore fix the upper triangle of $\Lambda$ to zero and constrain its diagonal to be positive, which enables identification of the loading parameters. With $D = 4$ latent factors and $K = 12$ measurement types this gives $DM - D(D+1)/2 = 86$ free lower-triangular loadings, $D = 4$ diagonal loadings and $M = 24$ idiosyncratic standard deviations ($\psi$), compared to $M(M-1)/2 = 276$ free correlation coefficients in the full correlation matrix. Loadings were given standard normal priors and $\psi$ a log-normal prior centred at 0.6 to keep the idiosyncratic standard deviations positive and away from zero. The models are otherwise identical to s8 (s16, multivariate normal), s10 (s14, multivariate normal), and their multivariate t-distribution counterparts (s17 and s15, respectively).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false

# This calculates the number of free parameters in the factor loadings models
D <- 6
K <- dat$d$K
M <- 2 * K

D * M - D* (D+1) / 2
```

Increasing the number of loadings to $D = 6$ gives $DM - D(D+1)/2 = 123$ free parameters and potentially more flexibility. Models s14 to s17 have been run also with $D = 6$ to assess the effect of a larger set of loadings. We include this run in the full comparison table below. Together the full comparison suggests that model s13 (MVT with time &times; type variance structure) has the best predictive accuracy. A small number of participants have Pareto k values larger than 0.7, but none larger than 1 (@tbl-full-model-comp).
<!-- REVIEW: In s13, 12 of 73 participants (16%) have Pareto k > 0.7 (none > 1); this is not a "small number", and the ELPD estimates are correspondingly less reliable. Several other models have participants with k > 1. Suggested: "In model s13, 12 of 73 participants (16%) have Pareto k values larger than 0.7, but none larger than 1, and ELPD differences should therefore be interpreted with some caution (@tbl-full-model-comp)." --> The multivariate models have better estimated predictive accuracy compared to the univariate counterparts and the robust versions (*t*-distributions) perform better than the normal likelihoods. Finally, the simplified variance structure generally performs better than the more complex structure. Together this suggests that the candidate model s13 is preferred for inference. We will use it together with the univariate version in subsequent steps.   


```{r}

#| tbl-cap: "Model definitions, variance structures, ELPD and Pareto K estimates from models s8-s18"

loo.s18 <- readRDS("fits/paper1/loo_s18.RDS")

loo.s17 <- readRDS("fits/paper1/loo_s17.RDS")

loo.s16d6 <- readRDS("fits/paper1/loo_s16_D6.RDS")
loo.s17d6 <- readRDS("fits/paper1/loo_s17_D6.RDS")



# Model structures

model_struct <- data.frame(
  model = c("s8", "s9", "s10", "s11", "s12", "s13", "s18", "s14", "s15", "s16", "s17", "s14-D6", "s15-D6", "s16-D6", "s17-D6"), 
  likelihood = c("MVN, full correlation matrix", 
                 "Univariate normal",

                 "Univariate t-distribution",

                 "MVN, 6 latent factors",
                 "MVT, 6 latent factors"), 
  sigma = c("time &times; type", 
            "time &times; type &times; treat",
            "time &times; type &times; treat",

            "time &times; type &times; treat", 
            "time &times; type",

            "time &times; type &times; treat",
            "time &times; type", 
            "time &times; type",
            "time &times; type &times; treat",
            "time &times; type &times; treat",
            "time &times; type", 
            "time &times; type"))






pareto_k_stats <- bind_rows(
  
    loo.s8$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s8"),
  
      loo.s9$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s9"),

  
      loo.s18$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s18"),
  
    loo.s10$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s10"),
  
  
  loo.s11$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s11"), 

    loo.s12$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s12"), 
  
    loo.s13$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s13"), 
  
      loo.s14$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s14"),
  
      loo.s15$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s15"),
  
      loo.s16$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s16"), 
  
      loo.s17$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s17"), 
  
        loo.s14d6$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s14-D6"),
  
      loo.s15d6$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s15-D6"),
  
      loo.s16d6$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s16-D6"), 
  
      loo.s17d6$pointwise |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
  mutate(model = "s17-D6")
  
  
  
  )  |> 
  mutate(pk0.7 = if_else(influence_pareto_k > 0.7, 1, 0), 
         pk1  = if_else(influence_pareto_k > 1, 1, 0)) |> 
  summarise(.by = model, 
            max_pareto_k = max(influence_pareto_k), 
            n_pk0.7 = sum(pk0.7), 
            n_pk1 = sum(pk1)) 




loo_compare(list("s8" = loo.s8, 
                 "s9" = loo.s9,
                 "s10" = loo.s10,
                 "s11" = loo.s11, 
                 "s12" = loo.s12, 
                 "s13" = loo.s13, 
                 "s18" = loo.s18, 
                 "s14" = loo.s14, 
                 "s15" = loo.s15, 
                 "s16" = loo.s16, 
                 "s17" = loo.s17 ,
                 "s14-D6" = loo.s14d6, 
                 "s15-D6" = loo.s15d6, 
                 "s16-D6" = loo.s16d6, 
                 "s17-D6" = loo.s17d6
                )) |> 
    data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "model") |> 
  
  inner_join(pareto_k_stats) |> 
  inner_join(model_struct) |> 
  
  dplyr::select(model, likelihood, sigma, elpd_diff, se_diff, n_pk0.7, n_pk1, max_pareto_k) |> 
  gt() |> 
  cols_label(elpd_diff = 'ELPD diff', 
             se_diff = "SE", 
             n_pk0.7 = "Pareto k > 0.7", 
             n_pk1 = "Pareto k > 1", 
             max_pareto_k = "Max Pareto K", 
             likelihood = "Likelihood", 
             sigma = md("&sigma; structure")) |>
  fmt_markdown(columns = sigma) |> 
  fmt_auto()
```
